Dear Readers,

Thank you sincerely for subscribing, commenting, and engaging with my work.

I started Beyond the Ideological because I enjoy developing and reworking concepts (most recently Third Worldism), connecting dots, and sharing things I find intriguing.

Unfortunately, my Substack has grown less organized and less fun than I would like, and I want a structure that is easier for me to sustain and, more importantly, easier for you to follow.

Starting August 15th, you can expect five formats:

1- The Meridian — A weekly column or essay on geopolitics, a crisis, a war, a controversy, or idea consuming the political and intellectual debate of the moment.

2- From Elsewhere — Every Friday, a short note on some developments worth watching across different sectors paired with selected links, books, and excerpts from sources that rarely enter the usual conversation, including Arab and Israeli media and publications from Latin America, Europe, Africa, and beyond.

3- Long Cycles — On the 15th of every month, a closer look at some of the long-term forces reshaping societies beyond the Western world, from political causes, demographics, and migration to technology/A.I. adoption, urbanization, and generational shifts.

4- The Palimpsest — On the 30th of every month, a translated short text from literature, history, or political thought that I believe deserves a wider audience.

5- Beyond the Ideological Podcast — Periodically.

The purpose is to bring together developments too often examined separately and to share more of the background that informs my analysis and conclusions. Geopolitics cannot be separated from markets, energy from industrial capacity, or political movements from the intellectual traditions that animate them. Third Worldism, liberalism, Islamism, technological utopianism, and other ideological doctrines also shape how events are interpreted and which solutions appear desirable. In this sense, I consider Beyond the Ideological a very humble effort to look at both the forces moving the world and the battles over how to understand them.

I hope you will enjoy the next chapter of this project!

Tech sector breadth is rapidly improving:

75% of S&P 500 technology sector stocks finished above their 200-day moving average last week, the highest percentage since October 2024.

This marked the first time in 219 trading days that this threshold was reached, ending the 9th-longest streak on record.

By comparison, the longest stretch during which fewer than 75% of tech stocks traded above their 200-day moving average lasted 759 trading days, ending on April 22, 2003, following the Dot-Com Bubble burst.

Historically, each time such a streak ended, the technology sector returned +2.5% on average over the following month and +7.3% over the next 3 months.

After 6 months and 12 months, the average gains were +15.5% and +33.4%, respectively.

Meanwhile, 69% of Nasdaq 100 stocks are now trading above their 200-day moving average, near the highest percentage since July 2025.

The tech stock rally is gaining momentum.

Everyone has a different trading style, and not everyones trading style works well with person to person. 

I typically have two trades I take and I stick to them. Those trades are also heavily context dependent. For example, not really having traded crypto for the past year. Just like staying out in prev bear markets is bc of the context/macro trends. 

One is a defensive trade, other is reclaim at what I call historical supports. But the reclaim itself isnt as important to me as is the history of the spot. The defensive trade is at a htf spot with a sharp sell off that isn't looking for a trend reversal but a lower high. While the reclaim is typically an end to end trade. 

Core postions are a bit different in the fact that something i have conviction in. The core doesnt get touched, but I will trade around the core on a different brokerage in order to. Llower the effective cost average, or accumulate more shares. The core itself is a longer term belief where as 90% of what I trade means nothing to me at all. So there are both low time frame, and high time frames trades and beliefs. 

I will post some examples of the actual style with context. But again there are some things you just cant really describe. Like gut. There's a lot of thoughts and feelings that go into buying and selling that you can't put on paper.

Where as having something that is correlated just ends up being the same bet you are already making in your trades for example.

A lot of really creative structures in terms of protecting yourself but still allowing yourself to play the game aggressively when you want. and then obviously there are a lot of tax strats you can implement. One of the interesting questions to ponder for this upcoming crypto bull market is whether the bear market winners continue to outperform. 

Previously, we mostly had new winners once the bull market got going and things that did well in the bear market actually ended up being laggards. LINK the major example from 19-20. 

One exception that comes to mind is BNB, which made a new ATH in the bear and ripped incredibly hard in 2021. Feel like this is the correct place to say Hyperliquid. 

Overall, I think crypto as an asset class is much more mature going into 2027 and beyond.

I think we have left the speculative phase, and therefore it's conceivable to assume that the winners of this bear market could continue to do well, as many of them are doing well because they are actually generating revenue, and it feels like this is the cycle where actual adoption is rewarded. 

I still also believe ZEC will be an outlier as it essentially did nothing for like 10 years, and has maintained a year long outperformance trend vs BTC, which is maybe a first for a project after doing so badly against BTC for such a long time. 

Anyway, food for thought, and worth not just blindly assuming you already have the winning bags because they are doing well right now.

It’s really interesting that there’s basically a bipartisan consensus based on complete and trivially debunkable falsities, namely that 

- datacenters consume meaningful amounts of water (they don’t) 
- datacenters are responsible for power prices increases over the last decade (they aren’t - inflation and decarbonisation in blue states is)
- datacenters impose costs on local communities (they generally enrich them and make life better) 
- datacenters are being built “for flock mass surveillance” (flock accounts for, generously, 0.01% of the DC buildout) 
- datacenters create noise and other pollution (they don’t) 
- datacenters are being built in residential areas (they aren’t) 
- datacenters get tax abatements that entirely eliminate their tax burden (never the case- abatements typically only cover a small fraction of taxes, and DC pay a half dozen different type of taxes that go to the state and city, they are always net and meaningful taxpayers)  

Virtually everything your conspiracy minded friend believes about datacenters is false. It’s also completely trivial to debunk using a simple google search or AI query but these people just blindly trust a random tiktoker sitting in their car instead. 

Are there real objections? Sure. But the opponents of datacenters aren’t making them. They rely on outright falsehoods like DCs are poisoning the water, or creating droughts, or tripling power prices locally, or paying zero taxes. 

Rare to see a popular consensus on both sides of the aisle that is basically a complete inversion the actual fact pattern.

Easy Money

Everybody laughed at Mark Minervini when he got caught on CNBC talking about a company he clearly didn’t know very well. But let’s be honest: 99% of people on X are exactly the same.

Most people here can talk confidently about 100 stocks. Ask them to go really deep and they probably know two of them well, if they’re lucky.

And I’m no different. When someone asks me about a random company, most of the time I simply say, “I don’t know.” Because I really don’t know anything of real value about 99% of the companies in the stock market.

That’s the point.

If you’ve been following me on $ZIM, you already know I believe the buyout story ended a long time ago. The government rejected it, the prime minister rejected it, and I expect the formal announcement very soon. Most smart investors already figured this out, and Israeli institutional investors have started buying again.

But apparently some algos, foreign investors, and a few people here on X who think they understand what is happening in Israel still believe there is a 5%, 10% or 20% chance the deal happens. I think the odds are closer to 0.1%.

So every time another newspaper article comes out saying the buyout isn’t going to happen, $ZIM gets hit again.

This time it fell to around $24.70. I immediately said I was happy to sell more puts there, and I sold around $33,000 worth of puts expiring next week(see below).

I didn’t need to start researching. I didn’t need to read 20 articles. I didn’t need to build another model. I already know the situation.

At the same time, anyone following shipping can see freight rates keep climbing and companies across the industry continue making serious money. $ZIM should be one of the biggest beneficiaries because its earnings are more sensitive to spot rates.

That is the advantage of knowing a few situations extremely well.

And this is probably exactly how the two hedge funds that helped found $WGS felt when everyone panicked and crashed the stock to around $35. They had a superior understanding of the company and the situation, so while everyone else was panicking, they could immediately put more than $150 million into the stock. A few months later, the stock had more than doubled.

For them, it probably didn’t even feel like a big bet. They knew the company better than almost anyone else in the market. From their point of view, it was taking candy from a child.

You can know 5% about 100 stocks and always have something to say.

Or you can know a few companies so well that when the market gives you a stupid price, you don’t need a week to figure out what to do. You can act in one minute.

$STAA Q&A + Earnings Report: Final Summary

$STAA currently has a market cap of around $1.3B, with $181.5M in cash, cash equivalents and investments, no debt, and the company is profitable again.

I went over the entire earnings call and listened carefully to the Q&A, and in my opinion it reinforced almost everything I wrote yesterday.

The most important part was China. Management said the Chinese refractive market itself is growing only mid-single digits, while STAAR is outperforming the market and gaining share. Growth is coming from both higher units and higher prices. EVO+ was already approaching one-third of China volume at the July exit rate, despite still not being available in every hospital.

They were also positive about the new competition in China, arguing that more companies entering the space validates the idea that the future of refractive surgery is increasingly lens-based.

I am personally always skeptical about new competition in a field like this. If you are implanting something inside my eyes, I want it to be something that has already been inside millions of other people’s eyes for many years. I don’t want to discover three or five years later that some new technology has a problem nobody knew about.

That is where STAAR has a meaningful advantage. Its ICL technology has more than 30 years of history and millions of lenses have already been implanted. A competitor can build a similar product, but it cannot manufacture decades of clinical history overnight.

The U.S. Q&A was also interesting. The small sequential decline was partly because STAAR was prioritizing made-to-order lenses for the huge demand coming from China. In other words, part of the problem was supply, not demand.

This brings me back to why I still think $STAA is such a unique strategic asset.

Imagine a patient walks into a refractive surgery center because he wants to get rid of his glasses. The doctor examines him and says, “Laser is not the best option for you. Your cornea may be too thin, your prescription may be too high, or for another reason you are simply not an ideal laser candidate.”

A clinic can obviously already offer both laser and ICL. But from the point of view of a large manufacturer, if you only sell laser technology, that patient is basically lost revenue.

If the same company also owns STAAR, it can participate no matter which solution the doctor chooses.

One patient is perfect for laser. Another is better suited for EVO ICL. The manufacturer can offer the doctor a more complete refractive platform instead of just one procedure.

That creates obvious synergies. The same salesforce can sell to the same doctors and clinics, the same distribution network can be used, marketing can target a much wider group of vision-correction patients, surgeon relationships and training can overlap, and the company participates economically whichever technology is ultimately used.

That is what makes STAAR strategically interesting to me.

It is a relatively small, unique asset in an industry dominated by much larger companies, and I think its strategic value to the right owner could be materially higher than its value as a standalone public company.

I still believe $STAA gets bought sometime within the next two years.

My base case for a future transaction is around $40 per share, but that number could be materially higher if the company continues to show meaningful operational improvement, especially in China and the U.S.

The previous $30.75 offer came when China looked broken and there was enormous uncertainty around the business. After these results, and especially after listening to the Q&A, I think that bear case is becoming increasingly difficult to defend.

Goodbye, Poseidon!

An epic 8-year, 8-figure rabbit hole in post-quantum cryptography reaches its dream conclusion. The Ethereum Foundation is abandoning Poseidon for L1, pivoting to SHA or BLAKE. This milestone unlocks ultimate security for lean Ethereum and foreshadows a golden era of hash-based cryptography.

Since 2018, the Ethereum Foundation has invested in magic cryptographic bricks, so-called "SNARK-friendly hashes". In 2019, Poseidon was born. It held strong and became the dominant SNARK-friendly hash, securing billions via zkrollups and zkVMs.

In a stunning reversal, breakthrough SNARK designs show that SNARK-friendly hashes aren't necessary after all. Off-the-shelf traditional hash functions like SHA2 and BLAKE2s can now match Poseidon in a SNARK. In hindsight the key was not SNARK-friendly hashes, but hash-friendly SNARKs.

The secret is doing maths over the smallest prime number: 2. So-called "binary fields" natively speak the language of bits, aligning with the boolean operations inside traditional hashes. This is a stark departure from "prime fields", where awkward large-prime arithmetic makes bit manipulation painfully expensive.

We're talking sci-fi cryptography. 1M traditional hash calls proven per second, on a laptop. Just 100x overhead vs native CPU boolean compute. Nobody predicted such performance, not even the handful of binary-field visionaries. Hat tip to the research geniuses: Jim and Ben with Binius in 2023; Ron, Benedikt and William with Flock in June.

With SHA2, the lean aesthetic of minimal assumptions reaches its climax. The EF's principled stance on pure hash-based cryptography has aged like fine wine. We now enjoy foundations the world can trust for decades and centuries, foundations worthy of the dream of an internet of value.

Speed of deployment is a secondary win. There's no longer a need to wait years for Poseidon cryptanalysis to bake. Emile and Thomas from the EF post-quantum team are moving at breakneck speed with binary fields. The strawmap now points to a production-grade leanVM in 2027, with CL, DL, EL deployments in 2028.

As AI becomes exceptional at cryptanalysis, the contrarian bet to avoid riskier structures like lattices and isogenies is visibly paying off. The past weeks have been brutal. Lattice-based "HAWK" and isogeny-based "SQIsign", both signature schemes in NIST's Round 3, have suffered blows. Sources I trust say more blood is coming.

On AI, the open autoresearch trend kicked off by ECDSA[.]fail is spreading fast, with amazing outcomes from zk[.]golf and SNARK[.]fast. Days ago SNARK[.]fast crossed 1.8M BLAKE3/sec proven on an M3 Max. Stay tuned for fresh autoresearch challenges dropping tomorrow.

Also tomorrow: Ethproofs call #10, dedicated to binary fields. Possibly the most noteworthy Ethproofs call yet. Experts leading the charge will present the future of hash-based SNARKs at 2pm UTC. What an incredible time to be alive. To witness history, DM me for a calendar invite :)

Today I can confidently claim that hash-based cryptography has won out for blockchain post-quantum signatures. SNARK succinctness compresses arbitrarily many signatures into one small proof per block. SNARK flexibility yields k-of-n threshold signatures, complex multisigs, and more.

Ultimate security. Uncompromising performance. Full programmability.

Believe in something. Believe in hashes.
